item.title: What history tells us about the Premier League table after 10 games of a season
item.description: Past years suggest it is tough to make big positional gains after slow start but that someone now safe will be relegated The Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged. Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38. Only 5.5 clubs per season moved by more than three places over the final 28 games, with almost half of the teams (89 out of 200) shifting by a single spot at most. Every club other than Arsenal will be looking to improve their position but they need not trouble themselves too much. History shows they will probably finish 2026-27 close to their current standing. item.title: What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
item.description: The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action • Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun ). But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.
